title: Albert Warner and Sonny Henry Interview, 1959-01-08

blocks.x: I think you might give your name first. Albert Warner. Any middle name? No, any middle name. Born

New Orleans, Louisiana. December 31st, 1890. I first started learning music with a half-brother mine. He learned from Honoré Dutré. Well, when he left, before he left, he bought him a new trombone. And a boy wanted to buy his old trombone from him. And he refused to sell it to him. He paid one against his brother. Well, he sent downtown, got me, and I went on up to his house to see what it was all about. I got there. He gave me this little old brass horn with about a bell the size of a saucer. A little chatois, a little French horn. Well, and I told him I didn't have time to be aware of that thing. So he said, well, you got the line. He said, I'm getting ready to leave New Orleans. He says, and I want you to take and learn this thing. I said, oh, I don't have time with that. Well, what he did, he went and put it together. He handed it to me. He said, well, blow on it. Well, when I first picked it up, I couldn't blow it. So he said, well, keep on. I just took the thing, kept it blowing in the first position. So finally, I made a note in there. I said, what note is that? He said, well, that's B flat. So he said, keep on blowing. So after I made that note, I said, well, he pushed it in the second position. He held my hand and showed me the second position. Well, I made that note. Well, then he turned around and shoved my hand in the third position. I made that note. Well, after that, that kind of made me kind of like the thing. I said, well, chefs, this thing ain't as hard as I thought it was. So finally, before I left there, he had me making those three positions. He said, now, well, what I want you to do now, he says, go down and buy your method. He says, come up here twice a week. He says, I'm going to give you this. How old were you? Well, about 22.
And, uh, had you played anything before that at all, like drums or guitar or anything?

No, never worried about music. I had the opportunity to learn to play piano, but I was a fast man at the time. Didn't have time to worry with music. See, and, uh, so after that, uh, I went and bought the method and started going up there twice a week. So finally, I got the first, second, and third position and learned how to make those notes in the end. So, uh, after he left, I went with Steve. Well, Steve, well, he wasn't a great musician. Well, I went on to him and taken a couple of lessons with him. So he played a trombone tune. Steve. Yeah. Steve. What was his last name? What was Steve's last name, Sonny? Arthur. Arthur Steve. Yeah. Yeah. That's his first name, Arthur. Yeah. Yeah. Arthur Steve. He lived right around here in Phillips street. He's still living. No, he's dead now. Yeah. And, uh, so I taken a couple of lessons with him. So finally, uh, Giles was putting up a band, Clay Giles' brother. Well, uh, after I learned, but before that, I got a self-instructor. A fella sent off to New York and got me a self-instructor. Well, I went on and I started a practice, not the self-instructor. So at the time I was in the pressing business too, and still working where I'm at, where I just retired from. And, uh, yeah. And so every time I'd blow the horn, I'd lay it down, I'd go press a piece. I'd come back, blow the horn, go back and press another piece. And my wife says, gee whiz, you say, you make me sick with this thing. I said, well, I might make you sick now. I said, but someday this thing will come in handy because I'd find out what it was all about. You see? So, uh, finally, after I kind of got good with it, Giles came along. He wanted me to join a little band that was putting up a little brass band back on that street. So I went on it with the brass, brass band and so they call it the Bulls Band. So I used to rehearsal with them every Sunday. So this same boy, what he was talking about, Pete, what we call him, being the pit, be a pee picker, huh? Yeah. And I used to go by Pete and Pete used to help me out a whole lot, you know, and he'd show me a different thing because he used to come around the band too. Well, what part of town were you born? Did you give that street? Well, uh, right around, uh, Sinan and Roman.
You lived around there. Yeah.

Part most of your life. I brought up around this neighborhood, right around what they call the Tremie, you see? Mm-hmm. I brought up around this, uh, neighborhood, yeah. And, uh, so bring back this, uh,
Pete you were talking about.

With Pete there. So we'd go to the barbershop on Bienville Street there and we'd rehearsal up near him and I just the bass and the trombone. So this fella, Amos White. That's right. Amos White would come along and he'd join in with us and he would write off a little piece of music there and make me go over that music, you know, and so finally I got pretty good with it. And so this little band formed up as I went with them. They call it the Bulls Band. So I went on and started playing with them. So first job they had for carnival day, Steve say, well, I wasn't good enough. He wouldn't take me out. So the boys say, well, he says, you better take him, would you say you'll have some kind of help. So he went on out there and then he'd come out there. He fell down on the job. You see, the next job that he got was down at the Holy Ghost Church there, uh, Holy Redeemer down on Royal and Lysian Field. So I went on down there and I played this job with him and went back, back in the woods here somewhere as they had, they were shot at a trumpet player and they pick up a trumpet player back there. So this fella walked up to me, he says, where are you from? I said, I'm from New Orleans. I said, I never seen you before. I said, no, it's the first time I was out. He said, well, you say you, first time you was out. He said, I don't understand. He says, you playing as good as this fella. Yeah. And this is an old musician. I said, well, I said, that's my teacher. He said, your teacher, you done beat your teacher. I said, yeah. He said, yeah, you done beat your teacher. So, uh, after that, I just going from band to band after I got good, you know, and I'd started playing with, uh, the, uh, what do you call this fella? What you was calling it? Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. So they sent downtown and got me, they were living uptown. So they said they wanted me to play with them. So I went on and started playing in a little, little band they had up there. No name to it, just the- Just Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. That's all. See, so I went on to playing with them. So after this, I went with, left them, I went with, uh, fella by the name of William, the Columbia Band. See, and after I left the Columbia Band and I went on, I went with the Camellia Band. Well, the Camellia had a pretty good pull around this town here. They had work in the countries and down Violet and all those different plays, Boytranville. They was doing pretty good. Who was in there who was leader? Uh, Joe Nicholas. Remember Joe Nicholas? Oh sure, yeah. Yeah, he was, he was with them then. Oh, Lord, that. He meant Louis Cabot. Well, that's not bad, huh? Why you call it that? I went playing, playing along with them. So I went with Chris Kelly and, well, different fellas, you know, I would go around playing with them. Okay, that's good. So, next band I got with was Kid Renee. Well, I stayed with Kid Renee a good while. And I was- That was the brass band or the dance band? No, dance band. Yeah. And I'd leave him and, well, when I left him, I went with, uh, another fella had a band around. Yeah, well, I played with him for pretty good while until got around depression time. When it got around depression, when I just give up playing, stopped all together.
I was going to ask some more about some of the names you mentioned, uh, Eddie Jackson on tuba. Eddie Jackson on tuba. People tell me he was pretty good. Was he really that good?
Yeah, it was the best they had. That's right.

The best they had. Because we were just too few. Yeah, because you see him, you could be, you could be 15 blocks off and if Eddie blow the horn, you could say, and blow that tube, you could say, that's Eddie Jackson coming. That's right. Oh, somebody was telling,
a big professor in that the other day was talking about how he used to blow down a fence now and then.

You see, Eddie, Eddie, Eddie Jackson, Eddie Jackson blowed, he had a different tone than anybody else. And you could tell any, any more, any piece he played, you can tell it was him playing it, because he played it different than anybody else. Yes, sir.
Did he do a lot of more notes or faster fingering or just louder or what was he so good at?
He's just, it's just a tonation that he had in that horn. I don't know, the other fellas looked like they just didn't have it.
You see. Listen, he didn't have it. Then, in other words, he could go up and get a note, regardless how it is, then. And drop down. Drop down and then come down. It's a big range. Yeah, that's true.
See, like he said, come right on down with that note. Like these fellas, there's a number of, there plays around here. We play it all the time, son.
But Kilman puts in a thing like that sometimes.
Lead and Savvy. Yeah. I heard nobody else played that thing since Eddie died.

Well, those breaks that John plays on clarinet, you know. That's for the bass to play. Yeah, I want to get that straight. That's for the bass. That's for the bass. And who would be good on that? Eddie Jackson and who else? Anybody? Eddie Jackson's about the only one I ever heard made that made it right. But of course, uh, Porter could do it. Yeah, Porter. Yeah, John Porter. Yeah, John Porter. Yeah, John Porter, yeah.
Yeah.
Who was this guy, Basie, by the way? Huh?
Basie.
Oh, Lil Basie.
Lil Basie was good, too. The little kid went, you know, a little bit of kid went to California by that day?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah. He was good on it, too. Yeah, yeah. He was pretty good on it, too. That's right. Yeah, Lil Basie. Yeah. He went to California. What's his right name? Did you know?
Uh. I know his family good. They used to live right at the corner from us, Sonny. Yeah. Right at Orleans and Roman. Yeah. Mitchell. Mitchell.
Basie Mitchell, huh?
Yeah.
I never heard of him. Bill, did you meet him out in California?
Yeah, he's a little bit of short fella, just about that big. Did he play trumpet or anything else? No, he played straight, upright bass and bass violin. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Hey, Los Angeles or San Francisco, do you think? You'll find him someday.
Let's see him. I believe he's in Los Angeles.
We'll ask Sidney Desvines or something.
Is he about the same age as you, Mr. Warner, or is he younger?
Oh, he's young. He's younger than us, yeah. Young than us, yeah. Yeah, he's young than us. He's, uh, he was a kid when he was around.
Around the street, yeah. Yeah, yeah.
That's old man Mitchell's son.

Yeah, yeah. His, uh, brother lived where, isn't he? His brother live here? Yeah. Well, his brother can tell exactly where he's at. Well, his brother on, uh, on Val Ray, right? No, but, but, but, but he is, yeah, he's that way. He even got places. Yeah.
Oh, catch him. Well, he can find out, uh, what part of California he's in. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, when you first, uh, learned on your trombone, did you learn to read right away out of that method?

Yeah, I thought you were by the end. Start writing, writing, learning how to read, because I couldn't play a thing out of head, see? And whenever anybody contradict me, say I wasn't making something right, I went to this man here, see? And when I got in the room together, he said, well, go on over it. So I'd go on over to a piece of music, and he said, there's nothing wrong with it. I said, well, they tell me I'm wrong. He said, you're not wrong. I said, that's why I brought it to you, see if I'm wrong. Yeah. I said, if you say it's right, it must be right then. I go back to the fellas, and I said, well, you all can play the way you want. See?
What about Kid Renee's dance band, now, did he play by ear, or by music?

Well, they played music and by air too, but they was better on this routine stuff than they was on music, see? Because a lot of time they had music up there, they just was guessing at it, see? Yeah. Especially the Sykes, you know?
Who was in that band at that time?

Well, the time I was playing at them, they had Kid Renee, Edna Mitchell, Joe Renee, myself, Manny Gabriel, what's this boy, what you say, boy, he put up there with you all? Andy. Andy. Andy. Henry Hardin.
What did Henry Hardin play?
Henry Hardin played saxophone.
Yeah, but he wouldn't play alto.
No, he played a baritone. No.
Did Hamdi play clarinet then?
No, he played saxophone.
He played alto too.
And they had another boy from Bay St. Louis there. His dad is a musician, Bay St. Louis.
What instrument? Did he play sax?

He played sax, yeah. And they had this other boy playing bass, what is his name there? Lazard. Chester Lazard. Chester Lazard. Chester Lazard, yeah. Chester Lazard. Chester Lazard, yeah. He was playing bass, yeah.
That was a pretty big band, that wasn't it?
Those were five. Ten pieces. Ten pieces.
Ten pieces.
Yeah, ten piece band, yeah.
Two trumpets or one?

They had, let's see, they had Rene, they had Rene, that, myself, Edna Mitchell, Joe Rene, Chester Lazard, Chester Lazard, and Henry Hardin, Thomas on guitar, and they had Manny Gabriel, Andy and this boy over the river, from over the lake. It was ten, ten pieces.
Who was Thomas on guitar? What was his name?
You remember Thomas? He lived on Sedan and Claibon. He used to play banjo.
Yeah, Thomas did.
Yeah. That's all I ever know about Thomas.
Was he related to Tom Benton?
No, his last name was Thomas. Oh, I see. Yeah, his last name was Thomas, yeah.
Who was in some of the other bands you played? What's more about that Rene band? Was that before the depression? About when was that?
Well, that's just a little before depression. They was playing upon their story.
In the 1920s up then?
Yeah, around about 27, 28. Because we played up there, it must have been about a year and a half.
Was that before Lee Collins and Rogashow and a bunch went in there, or was it?

Well, Lee Collins used to come up there. Well, you see, after they left from up there, then they started playing what you call percentage jobs, then they was using different bands, see? Then Lee Collins left here and he went on up to Chicago, I believe, New York, some of those places.
Somebody called that the Astoria Roof. Was it sort of a roof garden? Did they call it that?
Well, they used to call it a roof garden, but it was the same as a dance hall, you see. It was all...
All closed in.
All closed in, yeah.
Davey Jones was in there after you or before you?

Oh, he must have got in there after us. Yeah, after us. You see, because after I left Rene, I went playing with some other fellas there, some little scrap band they had. I don't remember what band it was. Then right after I left, that's where Beansy was running the place, when he cut them down, they went to playing percentage, you see, and that's where Rene left, you see. Then Remy had a band, he used to come up there, you see. Is that T-Boy? T-Boy Remy. He used to come up there and play it too. He used to use different bands up there after we left. Different bands he used.
He used in California too, man. Yeah, in California. I'll get out there again sometime. See all the fellas.
I guess I'll be up there pretty soon. Not to stay.
You were just going out for a visit.
Yeah, I got my son up there. The saxophone player? Uh-huh.
Oh, what was your half-brother's name? I didn't get that.
Ulyss Jackson. I've heard of him. Oh, he's dead. He died in Chicago.
Who did he play with?

Well, he used to play with the Excelsior Band. That was years ago, you see. Then he left. He didn't stay up very long after that. Then he left and he went to Chicago. He played with Honoré Dutré. You remember when Honoré was playing with Dick Selsior? The Trumont player? Yeah. Sure. You remember that big fella? Big papers that look like a type? Oh, yeah. Yeah. That's who I'm speaking of. Oh, yeah?
Yeah. Well, something was going to say, you are annoying.
Because Honoré Lloyd Tim, you see. Yeah, I understand. Well, after Honoré Lloyd Tim, he said, well, he says, you see the Albert Lloyd in how to play. He was a good one to it.
Yeah.

He was a good musician, he was. Who else in your family played? Well, I ain't got just my son, the one that's in California, that's the only one that played. My daddy, he played bass, but that was, whoo, way before Sonny's time. The kind of bass did he play? Bass viola.
I mean, in the dance band? Yeah, dance band, yeah. The string bass. The string bass, yeah.
He played with the bass up there.
Yeah, but he might have played with the bass, that's before your time and my time.

I just wondered who he played, in any particular band you remember, I didn't mention. No particular band that I know of. I guess he played with some of these old musicians like himself, because right now if he was living, he'd be about 90 years old.
Scrub band, you see, he'd just pick up and say, come on, let's go have a little fun. I guess that's kind of band he was in at that time, you see.

Yeah, those fellas used to have, back in that time they had a lot of old musicians, you know, like Jimmy Brown, that fella's name used to play there. Yeah. Jimmy Brown, another dude they used to play over here at the cooperators hall, I can't think of his name. Yeah. What did you see, at that time? It was, it was all, oh you wasn't, you wasn't in the city then.
Do you remember Billy Marrero, Lawrence Marrero's father?
No, I don't remember him well. You don't remember?
You don't remember the superior band?
I remember the superior, but I don't know Marrero's daddy. I know his brothers, you see, I know all the boys, but I don't know the old man.
You heard it, you heard him I guess, and didn't know him. I didn't know him, you see. Cause I'm, he was, had the superior. Yeah. It was really his band.
Yeah, I remember the black, where they had, back in that time they had the superior and some other old band they had there. They had a lot of old bands.
Remember the Olympia band, or Keppert or anybody around here? Do you remember hearing Keppert when you were a kid?
Oh yeah.
Tell them about what they used to call you. You remember we were talking about how people get your name confused?

Oh yeah, well you see, Keppert was kind of a little cousin of mine, you know. Well they used to call me Freddy Keppert. Oh really? Yeah, his brother Louis lived around on Perth Street now, you see, and they say, well that's my cousin, you see, well they call, they call him, call me Freddy Keppert. And everywhere I went people used to call me Freddy Keppert.
Did you look like him some too? Well I looked just that much. He looked that awfully heavy at first before he died, I never saw him.
Yeah, well, you see when Freddy started, he started off on the violin. See, yeah, up beyond Villeray and St. Louis, see. He was nothing but a little kid then. And from that he took up a cornet.
What was happening around Villeray and St. Louis? Was it a bar room or one of those?

Well, Villeray and St. Louis, well no, there was houses like, in one part they had a bakery and at the corner, they had a grocery and bar, and that other part they had a bar room there. Yeah. On the riverside. Yeah.
And would he play in the bar room or would he just stand outside?

Well he played, you know he used to play at home, but after he learned, you know, and he started playing all them different little tongues around him, you know, then he left and he went away. See? Yeah, he left you and went on to Chicago. I believe he left before Oliver did. Doesn't make sense. Yeah, I believe he left before Oliver left you.
Did you hear, remember Oliver playing here?

Oh yeah, I used to go dance by Oliver's music. He used to play around here at the economy hall. Yeah, I used to be at him and, was that the fellow here in California now, Kid Ori? Ori? Yeah. That's when Oliver left here. I was at the last dance he played over at the economy hall.
How did Ori play? Was he a head man or read much or pretty rough or a nice tone?

Well he had a nice tone in his trombone. He was a good guy for me he did back in that time as far as you know as I had an understanding. I used to like his playing, because everywhere he was playing I would be there. I heard him. But I didn't have no interest in no music then you see back in those days.

I heard him a couple of times, but I think he's most of his man. Of course he can play. You see Jim, him and Jim is all in the same style. Anytime he's sitting there they're going to play it. They're going to play it naturally too. But I think he's most of a-

Well what is he a real teen? Yeah. You see that's the thing I didn't know. I'm telling you right now back in those days I didn't know. All I'd know I used to just go to the dancers they could sit down there and play it. I wouldn't know if he was playing my head or not.

I know that he wasn't a man on my top or Harrison Bond. Lewis Nelson wasn't on the top of him. He was a good man. Just like Jim. Now what did he call me? Jim. He said, hello Mr. Jim. I said hello. But my name is not Jim. He called me Jim but my name is not Jim. I said Jim I said okay I said how you feel? Okay. Because he just said I and Jim is a brother. Of course we kind of feel with him. And when we talk we almost talk like sometimes. But he's no kid at all.
You taught him drum on and taught him how to talk too?

No no no. Not at all. Wait wait wait a minute. It looks that way. Wait wait wait a minute. God damn. Wait wait wait a minute. I couldn't talk oneself. How can I just try? I couldn't talk oneself. But Kicks let me tell you a kid. He said sometime when he and I get together. I said partner? I said I'm learning how to talk good. He gave me a lesson you started. I find him out sometime you see.
Well did they tell me that Sonny was Jim's uncle though?

No. Your uncle? No. We used to know Ken at all. Yeah. You did know him of course down in the country. Oh yeah I know him so long. Yeah. I know him. I understand first. I understand. Yeah. And I said everybody and I think I'm the his teacher. But the idea of him but then sometime he used to get to talking. I said partner I say you are learning good how to talk. I said just keep on using it.

stuff job after he got me to play one job well he did just like I did Sunday well then he say you stay here I said all right so I continued playing with him so after I got to making a lot of jobs out in the country the band was kind of going down they wasn't doing much work I started going to country and playing and Wilson was running a little candy stand and he didn't have time to be worried so I said well you run your candy stand I'm going to play music so when they'd get something they didn't want me to play I told him I'm going to country so he said well I have to get somebody to play so I said all right you get somebody to play I said well get Red he said Red play the trombone so that's how he got Red in the band you see you were in the band before Red I was in the band before Red you see do you remember his father his father had been I don't know his father no I don't know anything about his father one of the organizers of a real old band well see me I'm the only old old man in there I mean from old back I'm the only old man in there when did you join it do you remember about one year I wouldn't know exactly what year it was before the depression the time you were with kid Renee or after that no that was after depression let's see this depression at 29 must have been around about 20 37 38 something around about that yeah it might have been before that you see yeah long before that but I'm just giving a rough guess at it you know about around about that time you see well at that time we used to rehearsal up and down rampart street see sometimes the rehearsal in in the back of one ballroom and then next time the rehearsal in the back of a restroom she didn't have no regular place you remember the time Lewis came down here to play that uh that peanut vendor yeah well that's the time I was playing with I was playing with him then well that was around when around about 19 in the 30s anyway was that when Lewis was at the suburban gardens yeah what year was that that was way back 1931 then yeah yeah around about that time about the time Buddy Petit died you remember yeah when Buddy Petit died it's because we played Buddy Petit's funeral you see what you were in the Eureka when when you played Buddy Petit's funeral you see but uh for uh for the Lewis when Lewis came in when we went and picked up Lewis up at the L&A and depot there and that peanut vendor was out then at the time they was playing the peanut vendor they had people around there like that you couldn't you they didn't know what was what was coming up until they seen him getting off the train then we brought him through canal street there whose band were you playing with then Eureka's Eureka's yeah yeah I played with yeah yeah it had to be the Eureka's because that was the Zulus band then you see
I wonder if they had all brass bands or some dance bands running down there I heard there were several
bands down there to meet them or something they had uh they had one brass band and if I'm not mistaken they had one band in in a wagon like you know playing on a playing on the furniture wagon yeah
I thought maybe Kid René or somebody was there at that time yeah in a wagon you were with him

I don't remember what band it was that was in the wagon but I know we was the marching band you see and uh because we played we played on true canal street and brought him on up to the hotel there he was staying at that hotel on Julia and Ramport what do you call it the Patterson? Patterson Hotel yeah
had you just joined the Eureka then or had you been with him? Well I hadn't been with him very long then

it's about that time yeah who else was in the Eureka then when you joined? Well at that time there was Willie Wilson Johnny Wilson myself, Carnish, uh Flowers let's see who they had on bass drum I think little Jimmy was playing what? Groundhog? Yeah Groundhog Groundhog? Yeah yeah that's what that's what you mean they had to use call it they had another fellow on snare drum I can't think of his name was that Jim Mewkes is that? And they had uh if I'm not mistaken George Lewis was playing Clarence Black Benny's buddy huh? Yeah yeah Black Benny's buddy yeah I believe George Lewis was playing Clarence
well when did Schatz uh play with the Eureka? I used to hear

Schatz yeah Schatz was playing yeah Schatz was playing too there was three trumpets Schatz Willie Wilson and they had some other fellow playing with Willie Wilson when did Landry come to town? No Landry let's see no I believe yeah Landry was with him yeah Landry was with him because I used to kid land by begging a cigarette that's how I do that lick his finger he meant for somebody to give him a cigarette you see yeah that's where we used to get a kick out of it so when I first saw him do that I didn't know what he's talking about and fellow say he's begging for cigarettes yeah yeah he would be begging for cigarettes that was their lineup Landry Shatz and uh Willie Wilson Johnny Wilson on uh baritone and uh Verrett

on tuba you remember for that? Yeah I remember him. Connish and I and Flowers on that alto and they had them two drums let's see they had a clarinet I'm more sure if it was George Lewis. Does Flowers still live around here or did he move down? He runs on the base he runs I mean he runs on the ship yeah he lives down my way somewhere. I saw him a week before Christmas week. I wanted to get his address too you know he used to live around here I know didn't he? Yeah he used to live around the Vera Street here in the Maine. Not far from here. Yeah but he moved down below cause I see his wife sometime around by around St. Bernard Street yeah but he's running on the ship all the time. He's mostly on the ship. He don't play anymore no? No he don't play anymore. Doggone that's too bad. There's no alto players and no. That's no joke. And no baritones. No baritones you see that's what's missing in those bands those baritones and those alto and those melophones those French halls we used to call them. Was there any saxes in the Eureka band when you joined? Well no they had a clarinet and the peck horn, the melophone. Baritone horn. Yeah and the baritone horn. Johnny Wilson was playing baritone. Just after that, after the band started getting scattered out they started putting clarinet I mean saxophone and baritone horn like they got
cutting out the brass and instruments. The brass and instruments and that's the main thing that they should have. Peg horn in the band.

That peg horn in that baritone is missing. Yeah. Because they got some of that, we got some of that old music up there now if Red was to go through it. Show you that old music we used to play. I was showing Sonny a piece there at what you call it? Chicago? Tribune. Chicago Tribune. Chicago Tribune. Yeah. Chicago Tribune. Right over there. We got all that there. Red's got a lot of old music that we used to use up there. See? Yeah I saw some of that. All good music too.
He's right over there because at base we got to work and then he's no doggone well. If he come here with me I'm gonna be on him with this bass part because he's no rock that bass.

The bass part started tough on some of those things. Yeah. Tough. You see those bass parts there. Some of these fellas not fast enough with these fingers. See them fingers. They got their fingers too stiff on it. Fingers got to be super. Just same as theirs on the trumpet.

No it's heavy. You can't press down on anything like that. No it's heavy. Yeah. You got your finger got to be super. Now the other man can handle one of those. He can handle the bass. Now listen you see. But I'm gonna put him on the bass you see.

See now. See the irony of this. With your bass. You got to know the artificial thing. You understand. So if something comes difficult to you. You must know how to make one thing work. So you see if something comes difficult to you, you must know how to make one thing one way. You must know how to steer and do everything. You must take advantage of your instrument. Never let your instrument take advantage of you. You must always try to take advantage of your instrument. And so that's where I feel at all times. The thing that I see is easy to make, that's the way I make it.
The same way with the trombone, you see, this thing that you can make on the trombone, you can make an artificial note. Make an artificial note, you see, on the trombone.
Use that third valve sometimes and catch funny things, you know.
No, no, no. You're right. The third valve. And sometimes that first and third valve, it gets a lot of things too.

Yeah, but if you don't know it, how are you going to do it? If you don't know it, you can't make it, there you are. You just got to be guessing. That's all. Because even while you're guessing, the band's gone. That's right.

Look, don't be afraid what you're going to say. We can save these tapes and not play them for anybody. I say this is for a hundred years from now. You know, if you want to, we can put like a restriction on it, they call it, you know, and not to be played for ten years, you know, or something. So don't worry, just speak your mind.
Sure. You know what I mean? That's all you can do, you don't think you need to know. You see, Jim, just like you always say about Jim. Jim, he's my friend.
Yeah, we all know that. We know your buddies, yeah.

Yeah, but they all, sometimes some guy, oh, did Jim beat you? I say, yeah. Yeah, yeah, Jim, do Jim know more than you? I say, yeah, I don't tell him, I don't tell him. I say, good. I say, I say, I say, but there's one thing. I say, Jim, he makes a living more of a chair than I have. I have made my living more of a chair too. I say, well, what, what, what use for me knocking Jim? You understand? Well, when I've come along, I, I did good. Mm-hmm. You mean he might come up? But, and then this is the question I asked him. I said, sir, if a man go to school, I said, understand me very well. You don't go to school. I said, if a newspaper, if I can take a newspaper and read it and you can't read it. I said, who is the most best man? The question has not been answered as yet with me, with the first one. Oh, he can do it, but I said, answer my question. As yet, it has not been answered as yet.
In other words, if he get a check, he put a cross mark and you can sign your name, well there's a big difference in it.
Well, he didn't sign at this. You see, he's all right in his style of things.
He can play it.
Don't let him want to feel it.

You can play with fellas that can use you in those things. Me too. I like his playing. You go get with some other bands, like Up The Line. Now, you know when you go up the line, that routine's all right, but they want you to see too. Yeah. You can only say, I'm a trombone player, you see, and I can play. All right, now when you say you can play, they're going to get that music, they're going to put it there. All right, now what you're going to do? You're going to wait until somebody started playing? Well, that man ain't waiting until somebody else started playing, he won't see what you're doing. See? And you can't fool them people. They, they, when they, you see it all the time, we get up and you read that musician, this book there. Uh-huh. They sometimes calling for men. They want a man that can fake and read too. You got to do both. Yeah. Well, how the hell are they going to do? You can't, you do your, if you can fake and you can't read, well they can't use you. You can get out there and play with these fellas that, that know that you just can fake, well then they're going to let you go by with that. See? But if they ever get any place where they got the, all of them do some reading themselves, well then that's where you at. Don't pee then. You're handicapped. You're just like a crippled child.

But I'm going to tell you about Jim, about Jim. I just wish that, that, that, that I could play with him in a way of speaking, understand? Of course I, I know that I'm a, his superior, you understand? But, in, uh, his style of playing, understand? And Jim, if you ever get in there one time, boy, he, got to make you sick. Mm-hmm. But he, he, he, that man don't forget nothing though. No, he got a lot of life to it. I'm going to tell you, you, you, you can say what you want. Take care of nobody, see, Jim is a good, tailgate man. Mm-hmm. That's right. Me, I've tried my whole life, to, to, to try and make him, learn how to read like I could. But if Jim had learned the way I learned. Jim never even want to learn how to read. If Jim had learned the way I learned, Jim would be one, one, one of the best trombone players in the city.

I wonder, did Jim learn to read a little bit? He told me once he could read some, but I thought maybe his eyes, you know, his eyes aren't too good for reading without glasses. I thought maybe that was part of it.
No, his damn head.
He still couldn't read even the glasses. This, this, this man thought his damnness to buy him out of reading.

That's, that's the same. I wondered whether he really wanted to or not. No, no, no, this is the truth. I'm telling you a lot. Yeah. His head ain't right. But, I'm going to tell you, that's some good even players. I'll, I'll tell you the world, anytime you jump on Jim, you're going to jump on a man. With, with, with his band and you put in the team there. But now, of course, if he, if he's going to, going to come out with, with, with the Eureka. No. It's a different attitude. You got to, change, change, change your level. If you do, you're in a hell of a face.

Just like he said, he says, if Sonny is there or I'm there, he don't mind filling in for either one of us. Yeah, I've heard him get along pretty well. But if, he said, if either one of us ain't there, he said, he don't want to play.

No. Because it's inside him. You see, I don't want against him. Against him. Nobody. If I get back up. You understand? That's the. But now, if a guy want to come in and see what he can do. This thing, you know. Well, I'm going to try and do it. You see, when he, A party get in the party now. I'm going to take my whole line. I'm going to see what he's going to do. But if a person comes out. You understand? Be nice. But I'm sure. Again. My band. I'm going to let my band fall. For. Trying to take a. Revenge. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Or. Come on in there. In our band, that's what we do.

You see, like him and I, we're about the only two that I know of. Wait together. You see, now, like sometimes you might see me look over at him. Well, that means that I'm going down, you see. If I throw my horn up, he know I'm going to pick up. And if I lay my horn down like this, he know that I'm going to pull down. If he do the same thing, I know he's going to take down, you see. And if he put his horn up, I know he's going to go up. So that's why you see him and I, sometimes you see one of us down, one up. We understand. We understand this way. And we never let one another get out of step.
I'll give him that all the time. All the only this last time. All the last time he messed me up. One time I thought that.

You know, this last time he messed me up. He kept saying to me, he said, Ow, ow, ow. Him, hmm. I said, God darn it. Every time I come, I come on. I said, no, I see them tricks. I said, son, I said, eat you, eat you. He said, you know something? He said, I done made the humbug. I said, I know you made the humbug.

He said, I know you made the humbug. Yeah, that's right. You see, when I'm wrong, I'll give up. You understand? Because that's one thing to me. I don't care how good you can be wrong one time. Oh, sure. I don't care how good you can be wrong. I said, well, I said, it's me. I said, it's all me this time. And then the first time, since we've been playing, that I haven't gone, I don't lie.

Well, that was when we ended up around Claiborne and, what was it, Louisiana? Is that the one you're talking about? Yeah. Where we rode back in the car together? Where you had the humbug? Yeah, we all came back in the car together.
Yeah, the thing. The left fuel? Yeah, yeah. That's the one you had. Yeah, yeah. The left fuel, yeah. The left fuel, yeah. That's what you had.
In the old days, I understand they used to march with the right foot on the first beat, like one, two, right, left, one.
But now they're doing it. Now it's left.
The army does the other way. Now the young fellas that went to the army, they do it the other way. But what do you all try to do now? Left. Yeah, left. You all try to make it the left.
Yeah, left, right, left, right.
Some of the other bands still, in case you see some of the old fellas, they'll put their
first... Yeah, the right, yeah. I understand.

Well, I'm telling you, some of them don't know their right from their left. Some of them just don't know or care. They don't know right from their left. And you see some's on the right, some's on the left, you see. And that isn't. It's all mixed up.

Listen, I can tell you one thing. This is a band of ours, the Urikan band. You look at the picture, and I guarantee you, you would always see putting your left, and the eye, red, and out, you got the same step. You see, I was left with all that at all times. Because me, I watch them, you see them, I keep them scared all the time. I take my horn, I hit them on the side, I say, watch the step there. And then this time, he changed it, get on the step.

See, sometimes I turn around and look at a chick, you know. He says, watch it, watch it. I say, I got it, and I make my skip, and I got it. You see. You get rid of it. All I do is make that skip, and I get back in there.
When you started out, how did you do it?
With the step? With the step?
Left foot first or right foot?

Well, no. I tell you, they broke me in on that, you see. Well, they had to tell me, because I didn't know right from left, me. See, I didn't even know if you had to put the right foot down or the left foot, you see. Well, Clay Giles, he was one of them old-time drummers, ain't it, Sonny? Yeah. He was a bass drum beater. And so I told him, I said, well, Clay, Giles, I said, I even don't know how to march. He said, it's all right. He says, come on. He says, come in my room. He said, now, listen, when I hit that drum. I said, now, put that left foot down. I put the left foot down. He said, now, every time I hit the drum, he said, you go. He said, put your left foot first. I hit. He said, now, you get the right foot. He said, now, you get the left foot. Now, you get the right foot. Clay Giles allowed me out of march.
Well, now, you say you played with his brother, huh? Were you the one who was saying that?
Yeah, I played with Clay Giles. He had a brother they called Oscar Giles.
Is that Albert Giles' uncle or father?
That's, Clay Giles is Albert's uncle. Mm-hmm. I see. That's his uncle. Now, his daddy was, let's see. I can't think of his dad. 된된된 !

name. Well, we'll ask him. He'll know. Yeah. I can't think of his dad. I just want to get those guys. I can't think of his dad's name. I was going to ask about, in marching, the trombones are always out in front, but where does the tuba belong? Right with you or sometimes the tuba in back of you in the old days? Way back. Two supporters always be in the front. No, no, but some time ago the tuba used to be behind us because if you had two trombones, the tuba used to be back to the second. But now here up late, we got to show that we go three. Three in the front. But if you had only two in a row and two trombones, and then the tuba in back. Who else back there with him? Well, on this side, on that side, that's your tuba and your... Sacks? Yeah. Where'd the baritone horn go? Out through, Sacks, and in the back, behind me. Baritone horn back of you? Yeah, behind me, yeah. Over on the right side? Yeah, behind Al, yeah. With the tuba? Yeah. Oh, yeah, you mean with the old big baritone. That's right, with the tuba, that's right. Yeah, baritone. That's right. Where'd the alto horns come? Yeah, he'd come next. Next. Where was the clarinet? Were they... They'd come next to the trumpet, but the trumpet would be last. The trumpets last or the drums last? No, no, no. Yes, no, no. The trumpet would be next to the alto and then the drums. And the drums in the rail. The drums last. The drums last. How come the Eureka does it the other way now? They put the trumpets in back?

Well, yeah. I don't know if that... I don't know how Poisey's got that lined up now, but I noticed that myself. He put the drums in the... In the middle of it. In between... Between Paul and then, yeah. I noticed that myself.
In the old days, I understand the drums always in back.
Always in the back. Right, right.
I wonder if he had a reason for that, or...? I don't know.
Well, he didn't say what was his reason or anything. I don't know.
I imagine he likes to stay back there where he can keep an eye on the whole band. Yeah, no, I guess... That might be it.
He's going towards them all. Keep an eye on that time, you know? Yeah. So in case they get out of that time, well, then he could call them down.
That's the only band that does it that way that I ever saw. I wonder why you did it to them.

Yeah. That might be the reason. That's his reason. Yeah, you have to be, yeah. That might be his reason. You see, to keep the... When those drums get out of line, that he could be right there to guard them, you know? Get them in right.
See, I forgot to ask you why you were christened at.
I was christened at the oldest church in here, that's St. Boniface, Catholic. Well, that church now is not even in existence. It was back on Yalvis, Yalvis and Onsaga.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. And where did you go to school here?
Yeah. The Robertson School. The Robertson School. I first went to By Road School down at... Durbany and Governor Nicholas. Well, they used to call it By Road Street then, back in those days, you see?
Governor Nicholas was called By Road?

Yeah. Back in those days, it was By Road Street, you see? Now they called it Governor Nicholas. Well, that was an old break building was there. Now they got a new school there, you see. All new school there. See, well, way back in that time they had all white teachers in there. Mm-hmm. Well, after they moved us from there, they moved us up to Bienville and Robertson, old Robertson School, across from the cemetery. These were public schools? Public schools, yeah. See, then from that school, and then that's where they tore this, tore that school down, they built up the one on Bienville Street, they called it the Wicker School. Wicker School, that's old Robertson School. Mm-hmm. See? That's way back in 19... 1910. So, no further back than that. 1903. 1903. I wasn't here then. Yeah. Did you have a band at school? No, they didn't. They used to teach you music, but they didn't have any bands. They wasn't teaching you music in school. All they did was teach you the notes and things, you know?
Mm-hmm. Would you sing or...?
I had a great big... Yeah. They used to learn you how to sing. They had a great big... The blackboard, yeah.

Oh, you know, like them great big sheets, you know? Mm-hmm. Oh, yeah. them great big sheets you know and they had notes and things on there, learn your different notes and they'd throw that sheet over and get the next lesson if they had. It was just the same like, you know like they used to have some of these Sunday schools, Sunday they'd like to have those lessons on, they'd throw them sheets over, yeah that's what it was like you see, that's the way they used to learn you how to read music, but it didn't have any teaching the bands or anything, teaching the bands that just come up here lately, taking the long yard to play music in these schools. What did they have in the churches now?
Did they have an organ in the church or a piano or any instrument? Well back, you mean way back
in time, in the olden time? Well no, most of it was organs, they didn't have no pianos

that I know of, and what about in the country? Well they didn't have no piano or nothing to your voice, you know. See back, you had to get out there and tough it up, you understand? With your voice, everybody would get together, you understand, and sing together. See they

used to call them melodians, they was a red big thing and they had like pipes, you know, come up, and they had small one and then they'd go right on straight on up, some as long as what he is there. See they had like hole cut in them like, like them flutes, them flutes that you used to call them melodians. In the later years they started calling them organ, pipe organs. Well then they'd have a fella back there, he'd be there pumping the thing while the organist would be playing, you see, but he'd be back there, he'd be pumping there. See, as long as she's playing well he just had to stay there and pump. I used to do that thing. You did it too? Well then you know what I'm talking about, you know what I'm talking about, what they call the melodians, huh? Well this is a pipe organ. Pipe organ, right, pipe organ, yeah, they had them big pipes there. I didn't know you were a musician. Uh-uh, uh-uh, uh-uh. You didn't know he was a violin? He was a musician. He was pumping his way through. You know what I was talking about, eh? You just was listening and you'd find out what I was talking about. That old fella used to be back there, man, he had that poor handle, sometime you see he'd be weak back there. You see him pumping there, but he kept pumping till his top. Yeah.
I'm wondering about some more of the trombonists when you were young. Did you ever hear Roy Palmer? Do you remember Roy Palmer?
No, I don't remember Roy Palmer.
Played in the district a little.
Who were some of the trombonists when you first started playing that you heard?

I heard, uh, this fella, this young fella, yeah, he was, oh I can't think of that boy's name. He left, yeah, Zoo, Zoo Robertson. I was gonna ask you, just start asking, yeah, Zoo Robertson. Zoo Robertson? Well, he was a good friend of ours, you know. He was a good musician. Mm-hmm. Zoo Robertson, well, and I heard this other boy, this boy. Lord Dutre.
Dutre. He was a good one, too.
And, uh...
George Fields was a good one, too. George Fields. Uh, I must say... Another boy, uh... Ackham used to play, too. Ackham. Ackham. Ackham. I saw his grave.
This other, what you call him, they're this, uh, Vig Gaspar? Oh, yeah, oh, Vig Gaspar. Vig Gaspar. Oh, yeah, yeah. Vig Gaspar. Yeah, yeah. Vig Gaspar. Remember anybody named Baptiste?
Oh, that, that... Baptiste. Baptiste, yeah, yeah, oh, man, that's some kind of... He was here. I don't remember Baptiste. Baptiste still is there?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Baptiste Delay, yeah. Baptiste Delay, yeah.
Baptiste Delay, yeah. Oh, man.
Baptiste Delay, yeah.
That's right. Baptiste Delay. I think he was the first one to start playing drumming, I think. That's when I heard, huh? Baptiste Delay, yeah.
First one to start playing drumming, I mean, slide. Slide, yeah, slide. That's when I mean, yeah. Yeah, Baptiste Delay. He used to play all his, uh... Yeah, yeah, yeah. All his halls around here.
You're Morris French. Yeah, yeah.
Well, Morris French, yeah, well, Morris French, he come after all those fellas. He's young, so... Yeah, he come after those fellas.
He's good, too.
Yeah, he was all right. Yeah. Yeah, he's good. Dorito. Yeah, Morris French. This boy, uh... But I was telling you about that, it left you and went away.
Drew. Drew Robertson. Drew Robertson. Yeah. You remember him, too, sonny? I played with him, too, in the Allen Band a couple of times.
Yeah. Was he a... Did he play Barrow House, too, or did he just read? Was he?

Yeah. Yeah, he could read and play Barrow House. Mm-hmm. Yeah, he was a long-round man. He played down the district there. Oh, right. He played down the district some time before he left. Then he went away and he came back and he played down that wall and he left and went on off again.

Well, I'm too young to know about the district. What was that? I mean, like, what was it? Well, that was when... I never really got a good picture of that. Well, that was when you... That was when you wanted to be loved up, you see, go down there. Yeah. Would they have bands in the houses or...

They'd have bands in all them different ballrooms, like Tom Anderson's and Mason Street was in Bloom then, you see. And you'd catch a band at this corner, band across the street, band around the corner, band on that side, most every corner you hit, they had a band. You used to call them cabarets. Mm-hmm. See, like they got them now ballrooms and cafes and things, but back in that time they'd call them cabarets. What was Zoo up to down there?
I mean, who was he with?

Well, I don't know what particular band he was with, but he played at the lyrics a couple of times there with, what's that old man named? Robeshoe. Robeshoe. Robeshoe. Yeah, Robeshoe. Yeah. Zoo played with Robeshoe a while at the old lyrics.
I played that too. Yeah. Robeshoe. Yeah. About four or five times we were with the band. Yeah. It was a John Robeshoe band. John Robeshoe, yeah.
Well, what kind of bands would they have in the district? Would they have musical bands or would they have barrel house?

They had, say like, they'd have mostly string instruments, sometimes trumpets in between that they had like, sometimes they'd have a bass, mandolin, guitar, see? Yeah. Sometimes they'd have a full band, but at that time they had six piece bands, you see? Mm-hmm. They'd have trombone, cornet, clarinet, bass, drum, and banjos. They mostly would use banjos back in those days, you see? Would the string trios like that, when they have three pieces, would they play in one place

or would they wander around from one place to another? They'd play in one place. See, now like, say like if Tom Anderson had them. Mm-hmm. Well, you see they'd stay there, Tom Anderson would play, you see? Mm-hmm. And they had others that would, used to call hustlers.
Mm-hmm. You see? Well, they'd play at this place a while and they'd go down the other place. Oh, well. Yeah, you see? Great way.
But like Tom Anderson, Tom Anderson had his regular bands, you see?
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Was that being Nookie Johnson? Did you know him? Johnson. And Willie, Willie Jackson. Willie Jackson. Nookie Johnson, Willie Jackson.

Those are two singers. This old man. That old man used to play bass. I can't think of his name. Just died recently? Oh no, he'd been dead. He was a bass player. Well, him and Johnson and this other fella he was talking about, there's three of them used play together one played a mandle one played a guitar the other played the bass but there was the one composed that song about maestress waggon and vignon taking my function gone i don't know that how does that go see yeah there was a song there they had a furniture store there on rampart where i really want to know if you see that fellow come to you to collect on this furniture you didn't have money to pay well then you look guinea to have the wagon back up there to take your furniture so he taking so many people's furniture away from until these dudes just compose a song they said maestress waggon and vignon and take my function gone away they just composed so i can't think of the whole thing you know but that's the weather yeah you remember that yeah i remember that yeah because they were still singing when
you was back sitting yeah mr wagner's been in took my friend's going away mr wagner's been in take my
friend's gone yeah you know they were them three fellas the one composed that song this guy's been
dead huh oh yeah well that this is starts a guessing game uh johnny prudon's johnny prudon's well johnny
prudon's well johnny prudon's well he was a big tall fella brown

No, he's named Ed Brown. French name? You like a French fella? I'm trying to think of that dude's name. Roman Breaux used to play in a trio mandolin with a bunch too. Yeah. I can't think of that dude's name.
Somebody from Glenny's era, around the time of Glenny, huh? Way around the time of Albert Glenny.
We'll check into it. Somebody else.
He used to play at Tom Anderson's. His daddy was, used to shine shoes around the thing there. Daddy's to shine shoes and he used to play bass.
Did you know Bob Lyons, by the way?
Oh yeah, Bob Lyons, yeah.
What kind of musician was he?

He was a routineer too, wasn't he? Hell. He was a routineer, yeah. He was a ham. He was a ham. He was a big ham too. Yeah, routineer too. Yeah, routineer too. That's routineer, sister. Most everything that came from around Ramport and Padilla, around in that neighborhood, that was mostly... Ham. We used to call him jambon in French, that mean ham. Jambon, huh? Jambon. Jambon.
You speak French too. A little bit. I don't remember, but I call him ham. Well, that's all the same. Yeah. Ham right on. You see?
Oh, down in the country, Sonny, you remember any guitars or banjos down that way?

Well, I'm going to tell you, no, they didn't have no banjos down there. No guitar at that time. All you know is to blow and beat. Beat you with and blow your way out. You see? And I was in the bunch to blow your way out. Yeah. Trombone, bass, and baritone. I can play that. Because what's the difference is to... Mm-hmm. Is it the same clip? I know the trumpet, I used to play the trumpet, now what's the difference in the trumpet and the baritone? Is it the same doggone thing?
Do you use the same mouthpiece on trombone and baritone? Yeah, sure. Of course.

Same thing. Mm-hmm. The baritone mouthpiece might be a little small, but you still can use yours. You see like the one I used? Mm-hmm. You can use that on the baritone. That's the same size. The baritone, it's the same size. It's the same thing.
Did you ever play anything else?
I started out, started to learn baritone, but I give it up.
Tuba, carnet, you never tried it?
No, I never tried it. And I had that around the house there and I never did work with it.
How come you didn't like baritone? I don't know myself.
It's a sweet adjustment, that is.

I picked it up, they gave it to me up at the office too. Yeah, the fellow gave me baritone up at the office and I had it home there and I flew around and sold the thing. You see I was so busy, I had so much on my hand. I had my wife there and seven kids and I had my pressing business to run. I was waking up in the office and now and then I'd get out and had to jump up and go play a little music. I had a lot to continue with at that time and I couldn't put in too much time with that. No. I had enough time with, I tried to learn how to play the trombone. Uh-huh. Yeah, I put enough time with that. That baritone, I wish I had a learn that baritone you see, because that's a sweet instrument to learn how to play. And I want to tell you. Yeah, it's sweet.

It's a man too. Yeah. You see that baritone, you could be on your tours at all times, that thing goes. Now doing the thing, your trombone, you're going to be like that baritone. That baritone you got to wait. You wait from the beginning to that, because in that baritone, he's all over. He's with the trombone, he's with the trumpet and everything.
You missed that part in the Eureka. Does the sax fill in on that part now or not?

Yes, the tenor sax. He's really good for that. Yeah, with that baritone, he sure gets it. No joke about that. Paul, he gets it done out. Yeah, he gets it on. One thing, buddy, one thing. If he isn't there, I'm really lost. Because I'm so used to him getting in the process.
Like that piece we played at West Long. And that solo. Yeah, that solo coming in just like that baritone.
He's the only one can play it.
That is a baritone solo.
Yeah, that's right.
You see, I tried it with the... With the... With the...
With the... with stuff

segments.title: Birth and first lessons on a borrowed brass horn
segments.summary: Warner gives his birth date and tells how his half-brother, a Dutrey pupil, put a small brass horn in his hands and taught him three positions at about 22.

segments.title: Lessons with Arthur Steve, practising while pressing, and the Bulls Band
segments.summary: He took lessons from Arthur Steve, practised between pressing jobs, and joined Giles's neighbourhood brass band, helped by Pete.

segments.title: First jobs with the Bulls Band and moving through New Orleans bands
segments.summary: He describes his first jobs, then playing with Louis Dumaine, Columbia, Camellia, Chris Kelly and Kid Rena until he quit at the depression.

segments.title: Eddie Jackson's tuba tone and bass breaks
segments.summary: Warner and the others praise Eddie Jackson's distinctive tuba tone and who else could play the bass breaks.

segments.title: Basie Mitchell, the bassist who went to California
segments.summary: They try to identify bassist Basie Mitchell, whose family lived near Warner, and where he is now.

segments.title: Learning to read music and checking parts
segments.summary: Warner learned to read from the method book and had a reader check disputed parts; Kid Rena's men played partly by ear.

segments.title: Personnel of Kid Rena's ten-piece dance band
segments.summary: Warner lists the members of Kid Rena's band, including Henry Hardin, Chester Lazard and the guitarist Thomas.

segments.title: Timing of the Rena band and the Astoria roof garden
segments.summary: The Rena engagement ran about a year and a half around 1927-28 at a closed-in roof garden, before percentage jobs and other bands.

segments.title: Half-brother Ulysses Jackson and Honore Dutrey
segments.summary: Warner names his half-brother Ulysses Jackson, who played in the Excelsior band and later in Chicago with Dutrey.

segments.title: Father's bass playing and old-time scrub bands
segments.summary: His father played string bass in informal bands, and Warner recalls old musicians such as Jimmy Brown.

segments.title: Superior Band, Marrero and other old bands
segments.summary: Allen asks about Billy Marrero, the Superior Band, the Olympia and Keppard; Warner remembers the bands but not Marrero's father.

segments.title: Being mistaken for cousin Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: People called Warner Freddie Keppard because the cornetist was a cousin; he recalls Keppard starting on violin.

segments.title: Hearing King Oliver and Kid Ory
segments.summary: Warner danced to Oliver at Economy Hall and liked Ory's tone, though he was not yet interested in music.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Sonny Henry on Jim and trombone styles
segments.summary: Sonny Henry talks about Jim, a trombonist friend he claims to have helped learn to talk, and compares players.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Joining the Eureka Band and playing for Louis Armstrong's 1931 return
segments.summary: Warner recounts getting into the Eureka, Buddy Petit's funeral and meeting Louis Armstrong at the depot.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Eureka Band lineup when Warner joined
segments.summary: He lists the Eureka members: Wilsons, Landry, Schatz, Verrett, Carnish, Flowers and drummers, and notes saxophones were not used.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Old band music, bass parts and artificial notes
segments.summary: They discuss Red's old music, tough bass parts, and using artificial notes on trombone and valve instruments.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Reading versus faking
segments.summary: Allen reassures them about the tapes; Sonny Henry and Warner argue that a musician must both read and fake.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Sonny Henry on Jim, tailgate trombone who cannot read
segments.summary: Sonny Henry describes Jim as a strong tailgate man who never learned to read and only plays comfortably with his friends.

segments.chapter: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
segments.title: Warner and Sonny Henry's trombone signals and a humbug
segments.summary: Warner explains their horn signals; they recall a recent mix-up on a trip back in the car.

segments.title: Marching step, left foot versus right
segments.summary: They discuss which foot to start on when marching and how the Eureka keeps step.

segments.title: Clay Giles teaching Warner to march
segments.summary: Drummer Clay Giles taught Warner to march by hitting the drum; Giles's brother Oscar and nephew Albert are mentioned.

segments.title: Parade formation and the Eureka's drums placement
segments.summary: They compare old and current order of trombones, tuba, baritone, altos, trumpets and drums in a parade band.

segments.title: Christening, school and church music in boyhood
segments.summary: Warner recalls his church, the Robertson school, singing lessons from charts and organs and melodeons in church.

segments.title: Early New Orleans trombonists
segments.summary: They run through trombonists of Warner's youth: Zue Robertson, Dutrey, Fields, Gaspard, Baptiste Delisle and Morris French.

segments.title: Bands in the district cabarets
segments.summary: Warner describes bands on every corner around Tom Anderson's and Mason Street, the usual six-piece lineup, and Zue with Robichaux.

segments.title: String trios, the furniture wagon song and Bob Lyons
segments.summary: They recall singers and a trio who composed a song about the furniture wagon, then Bob Lyons the ham.

segments.title: Baritone horn versus trombone, and Paul's baritone sax in the Eureka
segments.summary: They compare baritone and trombone mouthpieces, Warner explains why he gave up baritone, and Sonny praises Paul covering the baritone part.
